title: the Samkhya Karika)
hook: who, exactly, needs to be set free? the Samkhya Karika's last surprise

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika's dancer, once truly seen, finished and left the stage. What did you let finish all the way to its bow? Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

Who, exactly, needs to be set free? A freedom story usually comes with a prisoner. Someone locked up, someone chained, someone who walks out at the end and blinks in the sunlight. A teaching about release has to meet the same question: release of whom, and from what? For days now, Samkhya has been building toward its answer. Purusha the witness, prakriti the dancer, the long count of principles in between. Today, on our last day with the Samkhya Karika, it gives its answer, and the answer is a surprise.
screen: `WHO NEEDS TO BE SET FREE?` → `RELEASE OF WHOM?` → `SAMKHYA'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise, in paraphrase. No one, the Karika says, is really bound. No one is really released. No one really wanders from life to life. It is prakriti, in her many forms, who is bound, who wanders and who is released. Remember where the line sits. The I-maker, the mind, the feelings of being stuck, all sit on prakriti's side. Purusha, the witness, was never in chains. It only seemed to be, the way a clear crystal seems red when a red flower sits beside it. Freedom isn't the witness breaking out. It's the confusion clearing up. And how does it clear? The Karika says it comes from practicing the principles, the twenty-four we counted, again and again, until a knowledge arises that it describes in three short steps: I am not, nothing is mine, not I. That isn't despair. It means that thinking, owning and the sense of me all belong to prakriti, and the witness stops claiming them. What's left, the Karika says, is a knowledge that's pure and complete. Its name for the goal is kaivalya, aloneness: the seer standing on its own. Look back over these days. The I-maker that says mine. The count, named. A bed made for a sleeper. Yogurt already in the milk. Two travelers. A dancer's bow. And now the seer, alone and free. Tomorrow we revisit Yoga, the darshana that takes this map and turns it into a practice.
screen: `NO ONE IS REALLY BOUND.` · `THE CRYSTAL AND THE RED FLOWER.` · `I AM NOT, NOTHING IS MINE.` · `KAIVALYA: THE SEER ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the red flower sit beside the crystal. Settle, and breathe. Let whatever is here come up: a plan, a feeling, a tightness somewhere. Each time something arrives, don't argue with it. Just let it be colored light near the crystal, and notice the crystal itself stays clear. Thoughts can come and go. If you pray, you can pray quietly while the colors pass. The bell holds the time.
The Samkhya Karika. Its last word on freedom: the witness was never bound. Prakriti is bound and released, and the seer is left alone, kaivalya.

Your line: the Samkhya Karika. Today, when a feeling seems to color everything, picture the red flower next to the clear crystal, and let the color be the flower's. Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: In Samkhya and Yoga study, the closing verses of the Karika on bondage, release and kaivalya are read with commentaries, and the image of the crystal beside a colored flower is used to explain how the witness only seems to be affected.

sources.ref: Samkhya Karika 62 (no one is bound, released or transmigrates; prakriti in her forms is)

notes: Last day of the Samkhya block (1171–1180) and a week end (days 1174–1180): the teach looks back over the week.

Karika 62, 64 (nāsmi na me nāham, rendered 'I am not, nothing is mine, not I') and 68 (kaivalya) paraphrased. Translations of 64 vary; confirm the rendering and that the gloss (thinking, owning and the I-sense belong to prakriti) is fair.

The crystal and red flower (sphatika and japa flower) is a stock image in Samkhya-Yoga commentaries (and in Vedanta); it is not in the Karika's verses themselves, and the script presents it without attributing it to the Karika. Confirm the source to cite.
Kaivalya glossed as 'aloneness'; this is a translation, not an etymology. Confirm.
